analysis.one_liner: Cancels federal oil and gas leases held by companies that collude with OPEC to manipulate prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Energy Committee: it was referred on July 25, 2024, drew one cosponsor, and died when the Congress ended without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let the Federal Trade Commission issue a final order against a company that coordinated with an OPEC or OPEC-plus country to illegally manipulate oil or gas prices. Once that order was final, the Interior Department would have to cancel every federal oil and gas lease the company holds and bar it from bidding on new ones. The bill died in committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, if it deterred collusion between oil companies and foreign price-fixing cartels by putting companies' federal leases on the line. It also would have taken federal drilling rights away from any company an FTC order found to be breaking antitrust law by coordinating with OPEC members.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers hit by manipulated gas prices

how_it_helps.text: If the FTC issues a final order finding that a lease holder coordinated with an OPEC or OPEC-plus country to manipulate oil or gas prices in violation of the Sherman Act or Clayton Act, the Interior Department must cancel each federal oil and gas lease that person holds and may not renew or extend them.
A company found to have coordinated with OPEC countries would also be barred from bidding on any new federal oil and gas leases from the date of the FTC's final order.

The bill names 11 OPEC countries (including Saudi Arabia, Iran, and Venezuela) and 10 OPEC-plus countries (including Russia and Mexico) whose coordination with a lease holder would trigger the penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that hold federal leases and are found by the FTC to have illegally coordinated with OPEC or OPEC-plus countries to manipulate prices would lose those leases and future access to federal leasing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal-lease holders found colluding with OPEC

drawbacks.text: The bill only reaches companies an FTC final order has found to have coordinated with OPEC countries, so its practical reach depends on the FTC first bringing and winning an antitrust case — a high bar that limits how much the penalty would deter.
Canceling leases held by price-fixing companies could reduce near-term federal oil production, which critics of such measures argue could raise energy prices before replacement supply comes online.
The legislation has no standalone enforcement: it piggybacks on existing antitrust law, so a company not already violating the Sherman or Clayton Act would face nothing under this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is deterrent: companies holding valuable federal leases would have a large financial reason not to coordinate with OPEC on prices, and violators would lose federal drilling rights. The cost is that it depends entirely on the FTC winning an underlying antitrust case, so it would likely apply to few companies, and removing leases from sanctioned violators could trim federal output at the margins. On balance it is a targeted penalty on lawbreakers rather than a broad restriction, but its real-world impact would have been modest.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey introduced the bill in the Senate on July 25, 2024, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
The committee took no further action; the bill's action history shows nothing after the referral to committee.
Only one senator cosponsored the bill, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies holding federal leases are better off: no lease-holding company can lose its leases or bidding rights for price manipulation, because the penalty was never enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal oil and gas lease holders

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote the lease-cancellation penalty for companies found colluding with OPEC on prices.

for.name: 1 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senators joined.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, marked up, or reported the bill; it died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes, so no party split is recorded; sponsorship was entirely Democratic, with just 1 of 48 Senate Democrats joining Markey, and no Republican support.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies holding federal leases
industries.note: Companies an FTC order finds to have coordinated with OPEC to manipulate prices would lose their federal leases and future bidding rights. Companies whose interest is preserving federal leases and production even while engaging in anticompetitive coordination gain from the bill's failure.

industries.industry: Federal oil and gas leasing industry generally
industries.note: Most lease holders unaffected by an FTC order keep their leases, but the bill adds a conduct-based risk to holding them. The industry's broader interest in untouched leasing ran against the bill.
